analysis.title: America Builds, Europe Pays: Apollo's Slok Charts The AI Boom's One-Way Street
key_insights: Apollo estimates the AI buildout, proxied by average hyperscaler capex over 2022-2029, at 1.9% of US GDP. That is above the 1996-2003 telecom and fibre boom (1.1%), interstate highways (1.1%), canals (0.8%) and electrification (0.5%). Only the 1865-1890 railroads (2.3%) were larger.

Per Bloomberg consensus compiled by Apollo, 2027 hyperscaler capex estimates (Amazon, Alphabet, Meta, Microsoft, Oracle) are $1,131B versus $495B a year earlier. 2026 estimates rose from $465B to $892B.

Trailing 12-month S&P 500 capex has more than doubled since 2021, while STOXX Europe 600 capex has been flat for two decades. US private AI investment was roughly $285B in 2025 per Stanford HAI versus roughly $20B for Europe (approximate, read off a chart).
Taiwan's ICT exports to the US are running at about 12.5x their December 2019 level versus about 4x for Europe.
US installed data center capacity was 52 GW in 2025 versus 28 GW in China and 17 GW in all of Europe (IEA). Data centers use about 5% of US electricity demand versus about 2% in Europe.
US firms spend about 8.5% of net sales on R&D versus about 3.7% for EU firms. ICT software is about 40% of US corporate R&D versus about 7% in the EU, where autos are about a third.

Only one European model, Mistral Medium 3.5, ranks among leading models on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, scoring about 30 versus about 66 at the top. Goldman's Asia desk notes China generates 24% of global AI revenues.

AI is 49% of YTD US investment grade net issuance, 87% of venture capital and 38% of high yield. US data center securitisation totals about $81B since 2018 ($17.8B this year through August) versus about $1.7B for the EU.
Through September 25, 2026, hyperscalers account for 22% of Swiss franc IG issuance and 10% of sterling issuance (both from zero in 2025), plus 8% of USD issuance (from 5%) and 3% of EUR (from 1%).

Goldman's Rikin Shah argues the US-driven AI capex boom raises the global cost of capital, which pressures countries without high nominal growth. He sees Europe as not an AI winner and likely to struggle in a high-rate world as the fiscal impulse fades.
Citadel Securities' Nohshad Shah warns Europe risks importing more of the costs of the boom without the benefits. France is forecast to grow 0.4% this year with debt at 119% of GDP.

Goldman IG credit trader Jeff Papai notes more than $150B of chip financing deals announced for 2027 and estimates about $275B of AI issuance at 7 years and shorter next year, or 20-25% of front-end IG supply. He sees a clear credit runway until AI capex debt creation restarts in a couple of months, with crowding-out risk.
23 AI deals of $3B+ totaling $378B have been issued since September 2025.

Workplace generative AI use is 43% of US workers versus 31.5% in Germany, 28.1% in France and 25.6% in Italy. Consumer use is higher in Europe (Norway near 49% versus about 31% for the US in Q1 2026).

US labor productivity is up about 23% since Q1 2015 versus about 5% for the euro area. The San Francisco Fed's utilization-adjusted TFP has drifted back toward zero, so there is no AI productivity boost in the data yet. Literature estimates of AI's annual productivity boost range from 0.07pp to 0.5pp.
Magnificent 7 profit margins are about 25% versus about 10% for the S&P 493. Slok said the value of AI companies rests on the promise that S&P 493 margins will rise.

Since the end of 2022 US stocks added $40.5T in market cap versus about $2.8T for the UK, Germany, Italy and France combined. The Mag 7 (about $24T) are worth close to double those four markets combined. MSCI USA EPS has doubled since December 2019 versus about +47% for MSCI Europe.

Apollo's watch list: AI capex revisions, early returns on capital, shifting bottlenecks, which models get used, the end of token maxing, evidence of crowding out in financing markets, and productivity.

Deutsche's George Saravelos says the biggest systemic risk next year is something going wrong in the AI ecosystem (safety event, failed IPO, disappointing revenues) rather than France. He calls it dollar negative and very bond positive, and under-priced.

sector_views.rationale: Apollo's data shows US capex, chips, data centers and earnings far ahead of Europe, but the margin and productivity payoff is not yet visible outside tech.
Goldman's Papai sees a clear runway for now, but about $275B of AI issuance at 7 years and shorter in 2027 risks crowding out other front-end supply.

earnings_insights: MSCI USA EPS has doubled since December 2019 versus about +47% for MSCI Europe, and 12-month forward EPS is pulling away (Apollo chart).
Magnificent 7 profit margins are about 25% versus about 10% for the S&P 493 (Apollo chart).
The article expects Q3 hyperscaler earnings and 2027 capex guides later in October 2026.

macro_indicators.interpretation: Estimates have more than doubled in 12 months, so AI spending is a rising claim on credit markets.

macro_indicators.indicator: AI buildout as share of US GDP
macro_indicators.interpretation: Larger than every past investment boom except the 1865-1890 railroads (2.3%).
Weak nominal growth with debt at 119% of GDP leaves France most exposed to a higher global cost of capital.
High debt plus weak growth is where market pressure is most acute.
The US lead is largely from capital deepening, not AI efficiency gains.
No AI productivity boost is visible in the data yet.

risk_factors: AI productivity payoff may not arrive before the debt bill, with TFP still near zero.
Crowding out in financing markets as AI debt issuance restarts, with about $275B of 7-year-and-shorter AI issuance expected in 2027.
AI ecosystem event risk (safety event, failed IPO, disappointing revenues) per Deutsche's Saravelos.
Higher global cost of capital pressuring high-debt, low-nominal-growth countries such as France.
Profit margins outside tech (S&P 493 near 10%) not yet rising.

tension_points.bull_case: US productivity is up about 23% since Q1 2015, MSCI USA EPS has doubled since December 2019, and the US leads in capex, chips and data centers. If TFP turns, the US wins outright.
tension_points.bear_case: The San Francisco Fed's utilization-adjusted TFP is near zero and S&P 493 margins are stuck near 10%, so the US would be funding about $1.1T a year of capex through a saturated global bond market.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Utilization-adjusted TFP failing to turn up, or S&P 493 margins failing to rise (the watch items Apollo lists).

tension_points.bull_case: Goldman's Papai says the credit runway is clear until AI debt creation restarts in a couple of months.
tension_points.bear_case: About $275B of front-end AI issuance in 2027 (20-25% of supply) risks crowding out the rest of the front end and raising the global cost of capital.
tension_points.what_invalidates: Evidence of crowding out in financing markets, which Apollo lists on its watch list.

theme_stances.key_argument: The AI buildout is increasingly debt financed and saturating global bond markets, with crowding-out risk as issuance restarts.
theme_stances.evidence: until the AI CAPEX debt creation machine turns back on in a couple months

theme_stances.key_argument: The US leads nearly every AI category while Europe imports the technology and the higher cost of capital.
theme_stances.evidence: Europe does not and will likely continue to struggle in a high rate world
